title: Module 5: Transducer Design, Construction and Types

questions.stem: Which statement best defines an ultrasound transducer?
options: A device that measures tissue attenuation
A device that converts one form of energy into another
A device that displays returning echoes
A device that determines pulse repetition frequency
questions.explanation: A transducer converts one form of energy into another.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: During transmission, the active element converts:
questions.explanation: On transmission, electrical energy becomes mechanical energy.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: During reception, returning echoes cause the active element to produce:
questions.explanation: Returning echoes make the element produce an electrical signal.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: A brief electrical voltage is applied to the active element. What happens next?
options: The element changes shape and vibrates
The backing layer produces an electrical signal
The matching layer changes acoustic impedance
The lens increases the pulse frequency
questions.explanation: A voltage makes the element change shape and vibrate.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: Which transducer component is commonly called the "crystal"?
questions.explanation: The active element is called the crystal.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: Which event represents the direct piezoelectric effect?
options: Electrical voltage causes the element to vibrate
Returning sound deforms the element and produces a voltage
The matching layer transfers sound into tissue
The backing material reduces element vibration
questions.explanation: The direct effect is pressure producing a voltage.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: Which event represents the converse (inverse) piezoelectric effect?
options: Mechanical pressure produces an electrical signal
Returning echoes create an image pixel
Applied voltage causes the active element to change shape
Tissue impedance changes the propagation speed
questions.explanation: The converse effect is voltage changing the element's shape.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: The term "piezoelectric" describes a material that:
options: Changes shape when a voltage is applied and produces a voltage when deformed
questions.explanation: Piezoelectric materials work in both directions.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: Which effect is used during transmission of a pulse?
questions.explanation: Transmission uses the converse (inverse) effect.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: Which effect is used during reception of echoes?
questions.explanation: Reception uses the direct effect.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: In pulse-echo imaging, a single transducer element:
questions.explanation: One element transmits and receives.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: Which sequence of energy conversions is correct for pulse-echo imaging?
options: Electrical to mechanical on transmit; mechanical to electrical on receive
Mechanical to electrical on transmit; electrical to mechanical on receive
Heat to electrical on transmit; electrical to heat on receive
Electrical to light on transmit; light to electrical on receive
questions.explanation: Electrical to mechanical on transmit; mechanical to electrical on receive.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: The strength of the electrical signal produced on reception depends on:
options: The amplitude of the returning echo
questions.explanation: Stronger echoes give a larger electrical signal.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: An ultrasound pulse is produced when:
options: A brief electrical voltage excites the element
questions.explanation: A brief voltage excites the element and forms the pulse.
tags: Transducer Function and the Piezoelectric Effect

questions.stem: Which material is commonly used for conventional transducer elements?
questions.explanation: PZT is the common transducer ceramic.

questions.stem: A piezoelectric element is heated above its Curie temperature. The most likely result is that it:
questions.explanation: Above the Curie temperature piezoelectric properties are lost.

questions.stem: Why must transducers generally not be heat sterilised?
options: Excess heat could exceed the Curie temperature and destroy piezoelectric properties
The lens would become electrically charged
questions.explanation: Heat can exceed the Curie temperature and ruin the element.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a synthetic piezoelectric ceramic?
questions.explanation: PZT is a synthetic ceramic; quartz and tourmaline are natural.

questions.stem: The Curie temperature is the temperature above which a piezoelectric material:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of the Curie temperature.

questions.stem: Which terms refer to the same transducer component?
questions.explanation: Crystal and piezoelectric element mean the active element.

questions.stem: The resonant frequency of a piezoelectric element is determined primarily by:
options: Element thickness and propagation speed in the element
questions.explanation: Thickness and propagation speed set the resonant frequency.

questions.stem: Which relationship exists between element thickness and resonant frequency?
questions.explanation: Thinner elements resonate at higher frequencies (inverse).

questions.stem: Two elements have the same thickness but different propagation speeds. Which has the higher resonant frequency?
options: The element with the higher propagation speed
The element with the lower propagation speed
questions.explanation: Higher speed with the same thickness gives a higher frequency.

questions.stem: A manufacturer decreases element thickness while keeping the material unchanged. The resonant frequency:
options: Becomes equal to the tissue frequency
questions.explanation: Thinner means higher resonant frequency.

questions.stem: A 0.4 mm element produces 5 MHz. What thickness gives 10 MHz in the same material?
questions.explanation: Doubling frequency halves thickness: 0.4 ÷ 2 = 0.2 mm.

questions.stem: A 0.5 mm element produces 4 MHz. What thickness gives 2 MHz in the same material?
questions.explanation: Halving frequency doubles thickness: 0.5 × 2 = 1.0 mm.

questions.stem: A 1 mm element produces 2 MHz. What thickness gives 4 MHz in the same material?
questions.explanation: Doubling frequency halves thickness: 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5 mm.

questions.stem: A 0.8 mm element produces 2.5 MHz. What thickness gives 5 MHz in the same material?
If the desired frequency doubles (same material), the element thickness must:
questions.explanation: Frequency and thickness are inversely related.

questions.stem: An element has a propagation speed of 4 mm/µs and a thickness of 0.4 mm. Using f = c ÷ 2T, what is its resonant frequency?
An element has a propagation speed of 4 mm/µs and a thickness of 0.2 mm. What is its resonant frequency?
An element has a propagation speed of 4 mm/µs and must resonate at 2 MHz. What thickness is needed?
At resonance, the active-element thickness equals approximately:
options: One full wavelength in the element
Twice the wavelength in the element
questions.explanation: Element thickness is about half a wavelength.

questions.stem: Resonant frequency is best described as:
options: The frequency chosen by the sonographer for every exam
The highest harmonic received by the system
The natural frequency at which the element vibrates efficiently
questions.explanation: Resonant frequency is the natural frequency of efficient vibration.

questions.stem: How does PRF relate to the transducer's resonant frequency?
options: PRF is determined by element thickness
PRF and pulse timing are distinct from resonant frequency
PRF is set by the matching layer
questions.explanation: PRF is pulse timing, separate from resonant frequency.

questions.stem: To produce a higher resonant frequency with the same material, the element must be:
questions.explanation: A thinner element gives a higher frequency.

questions.stem: What is the primary function of the matching layer?
questions.explanation: The matching layer reduces the impedance mismatch.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: A transducer has no effective matching layer. The most likely outcome is that:
options: More sound is reflected at the transducer face
questions.explanation: Without it, more sound reflects at the transducer face.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: Why do broadband transducers commonly use multiple matching layers?
options: They improve transmission over a wider frequency range
They eliminate the need for backing material
questions.explanation: Multiple layers transmit well over a wider frequency range.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: For efficient transmission, the acoustic impedance of a matching layer should be:
options: Lower than both the element and tissue
Higher than both the element and tissue
Equal to the backing material only
Between the impedances of the element and tissue
questions.explanation: The layer's impedance lies between element and tissue.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: A matching layer is commonly made with a thickness of about:
questions.explanation: Matching layers are about a quarter wavelength thick.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: In a transducer with several matching layers, impedance:
options: Decreases progressively from the element toward tissue
Increases progressively from the element toward tissue
questions.explanation: Impedance falls step by step from element toward tissue.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: The main purpose of coupling gel is to:
options: Remove the air gap between the probe and skin
questions.explanation: Gel removes the air gap.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: An air gap remains between the transducer face and the skin. The most likely result is:
options: Reflection of nearly all transmitted sound
questions.explanation: Air reflects almost all the sound.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: A stand-off pad is:
options: A device that raises the transducer frequency
An acoustic coupling material placed between the transducer and the skin
questions.explanation: A stand-off pad is an acoustic coupling material between probe and skin.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: What is the main benefit of a stand-off pad for a structure immediately beneath the skin?
options: It places the structure farther from the transducer face, in a more useful part of the beam
questions.explanation: It moves the structure away from the face into a more useful part of the beam.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: A stand-off pad moves a very superficial target out of the near field and into the:
questions.explanation: It places the target in the better-focused zone.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: Which function is commonly performed by the acoustic lens?
options: Fixed focusing in the elevational plane
Electronic steering in the scan plane
questions.explanation: The lens gives fixed elevational focusing.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: Where is the acoustic lens located?
options: Between the element and the backing
At the front of the transducer, nearest the patient
questions.explanation: The lens is the outermost layer, nearest the patient.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: Where is the backing material located?
options: Between the probe and the skin
In front of the matching layer
questions.explanation: Backing material sits behind the active element.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: The backing material supports:
questions.explanation: Backing supports damping and reduces ringing.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: Increasing the damping applied to the active element results in:
questions.explanation: More damping shortens the pulse and SPL.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: A transducer produces fewer cycles in each pulse. Which characteristic is most directly improved?
questions.explanation: Fewer cycles shorten the pulse, improving axial resolution.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: A manufacturer increases damping to improve axial resolution. What additional change should be expected?
questions.explanation: Damping improves axial resolution but reduces sensitivity.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes increased damping?
options: More ringing → longer pulse → broader bandwidth
Less ringing → longer pulse → narrower bandwidth
Less ringing → shorter pulse → broader bandwidth
More ringing → shorter pulse → lower quality factor
questions.explanation: More damping: less ringing, shorter pulse, broader bandwidth.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: "Ringing" in a transducer refers to:
options: Continued vibration of the element after the pulse
questions.explanation: Ringing is continued vibration after excitation.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: More damping causes pulse duration to:
questions.explanation: More damping shortens pulse duration.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: More damping causes the number of cycles per pulse to:
questions.explanation: More damping means fewer cycles.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: More damping causes bandwidth to:
questions.explanation: More damping widens the bandwidth.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of heavy damping?
questions.explanation: Heavy damping lowers sensitivity.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: Which component reduces ringing?
questions.explanation: Backing material damps ringing.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: From the patient inward, which order of components is correct?
options: Active element, matching layer, lens, backing
Lens, matching layer, active element, backing
Backing, active element, matching layer, lens
Matching layer, lens, backing, active element
questions.explanation: Lens, matching layer, active element, backing.
tags: Construction: Matching Layer, Backing, Damping, Lens, Gel

questions.stem: A "5 MHz" probe efficiently transmits and receives from 3 to 7 MHz. What is its bandwidth?
A transducer has a centre frequency of 6 MHz and a bandwidth of 3 MHz. What is its quality factor?
A transducer has a centre frequency of 5 MHz and a bandwidth of 2.5 MHz. What is its quality factor?
A transducer has a centre frequency of 4 MHz and a bandwidth of 4 MHz. What is its quality factor?
A transducer has a centre frequency of 3 MHz and a bandwidth of 1.5 MHz. What is its quality factor?
A transducer has a quality factor of 4 and a centre frequency of 8 MHz. What is its bandwidth?
questions.explanation: BW = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 MHz.

questions.stem: Which combination is associated with a low-quality-factor transducer?
questions.explanation: Low Q means broad bandwidth and short pulses.

questions.stem: Which combination is associated with a high-quality-factor transducer?
questions.explanation: High Q means narrow bandwidth and long pulses.

questions.stem: Two transducers have the same centre frequency. A has a bandwidth of 2 MHz; B has a bandwidth of 5 MHz. Which statement is correct?
options: A has the lower quality factor
B has the higher quality factor
B has the lower quality factor
They have the same quality factor
questions.explanation: Wider bandwidth at the same centre frequency gives a lower Q.

questions.stem: A sonographer changes the transmit frequency without changing probes. Which probe characteristic makes this possible?
questions.explanation: Broad bandwidth allows frequency changes with one probe.

questions.stem: A broadband "5 MHz" probe lets the system choose a lower frequency or a higher frequency. Which pairing is correct?
options: Lower frequency for better resolution; higher for deeper penetration
Lower frequency for better PRF; higher for better duty factor
Lower frequency for deeper penetration; higher for better resolution
questions.explanation: Lower frequency penetrates deeper; higher gives better resolution.

questions.stem: Which imaging technique requires a transducer able to transmit and receive different frequency ranges?
questions.explanation: Tissue harmonic imaging needs broadband transmit and receive.

questions.stem: Short pulses are associated with:
questions.explanation: Short pulses go with wide bandwidth.

questions.stem: Increasing damping has what effect on quality factor?
questions.explanation: More damping widens bandwidth and lowers Q.

questions.stem: A high-quality-factor transducer typically produces:
options: Longer pulses and poorer axial resolution
questions.explanation: High Q gives longer pulses and poorer axial resolution.

questions.stem: Quality factor has which units?
questions.explanation: Q is a ratio of frequencies, so unitless.

questions.stem: How does a phased-array transducer steer the beam?
options: By changing propagation speed in the matching layer
By applying small timing differences to element excitation
questions.explanation: Small timing differences steer the beam electronically.

questions.stem: Which combination is most characteristic of a linear-array transducer?
options: Long internal shaft and circular image
questions.explanation: Linear arrays have a wide footprint and rectangular image.

questions.stem: What is an important advantage of a curvilinear transducer over a linear transducer for abdominal imaging?
options: Wider field of view at greater depth
questions.explanation: Curvilinear arrays give a wider field of view at depth.

questions.stem: Which transducer is most appropriate for imaging a superficial carotid artery?
questions.explanation: A high-frequency linear probe suits the superficial carotid.

questions.stem: Which transducer is most appropriate for a routine adult abdominal examination?
questions.explanation: A low-frequency curvilinear probe suits routine abdominal imaging.

questions.stem: A sonographer must image the heart through a narrow intercostal window. Which transducer is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A phased array fits a narrow intercostal window.

questions.stem: Why can an endocavitary transducer typically operate at a higher frequency than a transabdominal probe?
options: Sound travels faster inside a body cavity
The probe is positioned closer to the anatomy
Endocavitary probes have no matching layer
questions.explanation: Being close to the anatomy allows higher frequency.

questions.stem: A sonographer chooses between a 3 MHz and a 10 MHz probe for a deep abdominal structure. Which gives better penetration?
questions.explanation: Lower frequency penetrates better.

questions.stem: Lower frequency generally provides:
questions.explanation: Lower frequency gives better penetration.

questions.stem: Higher frequency generally provides:
options: Better axial resolution but less penetration
Better penetration but poorer axial resolution
Both better penetration and better resolution
questions.explanation: Higher frequency gives better axial resolution but less penetration.

questions.stem: Which transducer is best suited to superficial structures such as the thyroid?
questions.explanation: A high-frequency linear probe suits small superficial parts.

questions.stem: A phased-array transducer is characterised by a:
questions.explanation: Phased arrays have a small footprint.

questions.stem: Which statement about linear arrays is correct?
options: They are used for superficial structures such as vessels
They are used for transthoracic echocardiography through the ribs
They always use the lowest available frequency
questions.explanation: Linear arrays are used for vessels and other superficial structures.

questions.stem: A curvilinear transducer produces an image that is:
questions.explanation: Curvilinear images are curved and fan-shaped.

questions.stem: A phased-array transducer produces an image that is:
questions.explanation: Phased arrays give a sector image.

questions.stem: Which is an endocavitary application?
questions.explanation: Transvaginal imaging uses an endocavitary probe.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a CMUT?
options: It uses microscopic vibrating membranes manufactured on silicon
It uses a conventional PZT crystal only
It can transmit but not receive
questions.explanation: CMUTs use tiny vibrating membranes made on silicon.

questions.stem: Which potential advantage is associated with CMUT technology?
options: Broad bandwidth and easier integration with electronics
questions.explanation: CMUTs offer broad bandwidth and easy electronics integration.

questions.stem: How does a CMUT differ from a conventional transducer?
options: It uses a thicker PZT element
It has no backing or matching layer
It cannot be used in arrays
It uses capacitive vibration of membranes rather than a piezoelectric crystal
questions.explanation: CMUTs use capacitive membranes instead of a piezoelectric crystal.

questions.stem: Why does cardiac imaging call for a small-footprint transducer?
questions.explanation: A small footprint fits between the ribs.

questions.stem: Which factors guide transducer choice?
options: Depth of the anatomy, required penetration, footprint and acoustic window
questions.explanation: Depth, penetration, footprint and acoustic window guide the choice.

questions.stem: Why is a low-frequency probe chosen for a deep structure?
questions.explanation: Lower frequency penetrates deeper.
